Slide 2: Why replicate? (Data replication motivation)

What the slide says

Why replicate?

Slide 2
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 74%

The slide is setting up the motivation for using data replication in distributed systems: it is used to (1) tolerate failures by keeping multiple copies so the system can continue despite faults, and (2) improve performance by placing data closer to where clients are. But replication introduces a core challenge: copies must be kept consistent—i.e., clients must know what they see “in the meantime,” and the system must define how/when replicas converge (consistency models). Because updates must sometimes be applied to multiple copies (and failures may occur mid-update), replication protocols become nontrivial: they must be correct/robust and efficient, and they often require mechanisms that coordinate writes (e.g., serialization/atomicity and coherence with quorum-style approaches). This motivates the later discussion of replication strategies (leader-follower, multi-leader, etc.) and consistency models (from strong to eventual consistency), tied to the CAP theorem trade-offs.

Slide 2 · 11.4: Data Replication Strategies and Consistency Models › 11.4: Data Replication Strategies and Consistency Models · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra · Consistency.Print.book · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities

  • Primary reasons to replicate: fault tolerance + performance

    • In distributed cloud systems, “data replication is essential for both fault tolerance and performance.”
    • The performance motivation includes “placing data closer to users.”
    • This explains the question “Why replicate?”: multiple replicas provide redundancy against failures (fault tolerance) and can reduce access latency (performance).
    • (Evidence: replication is essential for fault tolerance and performance; also discusses placing data closer to users.)

  • What replication immediately creates: the consistency problem

    • Replication “gives rise to the challenge of data consistency.”
    • The consistency challenge has two parts:
      1. Eventual agreement requirement: “ensuring that all copies of data eventually agree.”
      2. In-the-meantime semantics: “defining what clients see in the meantime.”
    • This is why the slide’s motivation is not just about redundancy: replication forces the system to choose a consistency model.
    • (Evidence: replication → data consistency challenge; eventual agreement + client observations while updates are in progress.)

  • Replication strategies and consistency models are the “how” after the “why”

    • The evidence states that the section “discusses common replication strategies (leader-follower, multi-leader, etc.)” and “dive[s] into consistency models ranging from strong consistency to eventual consistency.”
    • So the slide’s motivation (“Why replicate?”) sets up that later material:
      • You replicate using some strategy (who leads/coordinates updates).
      • You expose some consistency behavior during reads/writes (strong vs eventual).
    • (Evidence: explicit list of replication strategies and the range of consistency models.)

  • Why the protocols are complicated: decay suppression + failures during updates

    • Replication schemes “can be surprisingly complicated.”
    • A key reason given is that the purpose of replication is to “suppress unintended changes to the data caused by random decay.”
    • But suppressing decay also complicates intended updates:
      • you “must now update more than one copy,” and
      • you must “be prepared for the possibility of a failure in the midst of that update.”
    • If updates are frequent, protocols must be not only correct/robust but also efficient.
    • (Evidence: decay suppression as the primary reason for complexity; updates require multiple copies and handling failure mid-update; frequent updates require efficiency.)

  • Performance trade-off interacts with the consistency requirement

    • Because “multiple replicas can usually be read and written concurrently,” replication can enhance overall system performance.
    • But that performance enhancement can itself complicate the design, “interact[ing] strongly with a requirement for strict consistency.”
    • (Evidence: concurrency enables performance, but it conflicts with strict consistency requirements.)

  • How coordination mechanisms relate to “maintaining consistent replicas”

    • The evidence describes that when using replica schemes, a “practical quorum scheme requires some additional before-or-after atomicity mechanism that serializes writes and ensures that no write begins until the previous write has sufficiently propagated to ensure coherence.”
    • The complexity depends on system configuration:
      • If all reading/updating originates at a single site, “a simple sequencer at that site can provide the needed atomicity.”
      • If reads come from many sources but updates originate at a single site, the updating site can assign “a version number” to each update, and reading sites can verify they read the newest consistent set.
      • If updates can originate from many sites, you may need a “distributed sequencer implementation” for atomicity.
    • This ties back to the slide’s “why replicate” motivation: replication only solves failure/performance goals if there is a mechanism to keep replicas coherent according to the chosen consistency behavior.
    • (Evidence: quorum + atomicity/serialization requirements; different configurations enable different coordination mechanisms.)

  • Examples of replication management approaches (to show what “replication strategies” mean in practice)

    • The evidence describes a systematic technique called the replicated state machine:
      • identify the data with the state of a finite state machine;
      • use the machine inputs as the updates to be made;
      • run the state machine so it makes the “appropriate changes to the data.”
      • maintain identical replicas by co-locating “a replica of the state machine” with each data replica and sending “the same inputs to each state machine.”
      • it also describes modularization: one module implements a consensus-achieving algorithm; another set runs the state machines to apply updates; and a third module reconciles replicas to ensure they remain identical.
    • It also contrasts with a simpler master/slave approach when stricter coordination isn’t required everywhere:
      • perform updates at one site (master), generate a new version, and “somehow bring the other replicas into line.”
      • the simplest brute-force version “send[s] a copy of this new version of the data to each of the other replica sites, completely replacing their previous copies.”
      • this works well when updates are occasional and the application can tolerate “temporary inconsistency,” for instance by requiring reads from the master.
    • These examples directly support what the slide is foreshadowing: replication is not a single thing—it uses strategies and management techniques, which then determine consistency behavior.
    • (Evidence: replicated state machine idea + modularization; master/slave brute force and when temporary inconsistency is acceptable.)

  • CAP theorem connection (why consistency choices are tied to availability/partitions)

    • The evidence states the discussion will relate to “the famous CAP Theorem” which “describes the trade-offs between Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.”
    • That connection explains why the slide’s motivation (“Why replicate?”) ultimately leads to consistency modeling: choices about consistency are intertwined with availability under partitions.
    • (Evidence: explicit mention of CAP theorem and its trade-offs.)

Slide 3: Availability, Latency, Durability (distributed replication metrics)

What the slide says

Availability Latency Durability

Slide 3
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 62%

The slide is introducing the three key objectives/metrics used to reason about distributed replication systems:

  • Availability: whether operations (especially reads/writes) can still succeed when some replicas/sites are down.
  • Latency: how long it takes for operations to complete, affected by the communication delays and unreliability of distant replicas.
  • Durability: whether data that was committed (or accepted as correct) remains safe/usable even after failures, which is supported by techniques such as replica separation plus integrity verification using local information and witnesses/hashes and agreement rules (e.g., majorities/quorums).

This framing motivates design tradeoffs (e.g., quorum choices) because you can bias the system toward better read availability vs write availability, while communication distance tends to increase latency and can force asynchronous replica writing to achieve acceptable performance.

Slide 3 · Consistency.Print.book · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Maintaining Data Integrity · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities

Availability

What “availability” means here: whether a read or write can be successful despite replica outages.

How the reading/writing success condition is determined: some systems use quorums, with separate read quorum (Q_r) and write quorum (Q_w). The scheme “declares a write to be confirmed after writing to at least a write quorum, (Q_w), of replicas” and a read to be successful if “at least a read quorum, (Q_r), agree on the data or witness value.” (It also continues propagating writes afterward.)

How outages affect success: by varying (Q_r) and (Q_w), the system can “bias availability in favor of either reads or writes in the face of multiple replica outages.” Intuitively, if enough replicas remain reachable to satisfy the required quorum size, the operation can complete successfully.

Concrete example from the book text: with (N_{replicas}=5), a configuration can be set so that:

  • a successful write requires enough replicas to meet (Q_w) (e.g., “a success­ful write requires that at least 4 of the 5 replicas be available”), while
  • a read can succeed with fewer available replicas (e.g., “a read will succeed if only 2 of the replicas are available and agree”).

Why this matters for distributed replication: availability is not just about “more replicas”; it’s about how many replicas you require to confirm a write vs to answer a read. Quorum parameters let the designer decide whether to favor continuing to serve reads or continuing to confirm writes during failures.

Availability vs durability interaction (in the slide’s grouping): quorum-based availability relies on having enough replicas to agree on the data/witness, and the slide’s durability objective relates to whether those agreed-upon values remain safe and trustworthy after failures.

Consistency.Print.book

Latency

What “latency” means here: the time cost of communicating between replica sites, which affects whether replicas can be written synchronously.

The key mechanism mentioned: when replicas are geographically separated, “communication with distant points has high latency and is also inherently unreliable.” That combination “make[s] it problematic to write the replicas synchronously.”

How systems respond: because of latency/unreliability, “When replicas are made asynchronously, one of the replicas (usually the first replica to be written) is identified as the primary copy, and the site that writes it is called the master. The remaining replicas are called backup copies, and the sites that write them are called slaves.”

So latency pressures the system toward designs where it does not wait for geographically distant replicas in a synchronous manner; instead, it writes primary first and propagates to backups asynchronously.

Why this matters: latency is a direct driver of the replication strategy (synchronous vs asynchronous). If you choose to require synchronous updates everywhere, the high-latency links between sites would prevent timely completion of operations; asynchronous replica writing helps operations complete with reasonable timing even when distant links are slow/unreliable.

4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra

Durability

What “durability” means here: after failures, whether data integrity is preserved and whether the system can still detect/confirm correct data state.

1) Durability depends on independently surviving replica failures (replica separation): the text discusses a “durability mantra” that suggests “imposing physical and administrative separation of replicas to make threats to their integrity more independent.”

2) Durability also requires integrity checking using only local or communicated evidence:

  • The text explains that if replication is done in simple/enhanced schemes that consult only one replica site, then “loss of data integrity… must be detected using just information local to that site,” possibly using “a witness stored at the replica site.”
  • It also provides a more reliable approach: a client can obtain “a second copy (or a witness) from a different replica site.” If the copy (or witness/hash) from another site matches the first, “confidence in the integrity of the data can be quite high.”

3) Agreement (majority/quorum) boosts durability confidence: the text extends this to compare several replicas/witnesses: even when there are disagreements, “if a majority of the replicas or witnesses agree, the client can still accept the data with confidence,” possibly reporting reconciliation needs.

4) Witnesses (hash-based) support integrity confirmation: the book describes “An alternative and less costly method… [that] is to calculate a witness of the contents of a replica and transmit just that witness from one site to another.” A usual witness form is “a hash value… calculated over the content of the replica.” With appropriate hash choice and witness length, “the probability that a damaged replica will have a hash value that matches the witness can be made arbitrarily small,” so “A witness can thus stand in for a replica for purposes of confirming data integrity or detecting its loss.”

Why this matters for the slide’s overall triad: durability is paired with availability and latency because replication designs must simultaneously:

  • survive failures while keeping data integrity trustworthy (durability),
  • still respond despite outages (availability), and
  • operate within reasonable time costs despite network/communication delays (latency).
4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Maintaining Data Integrity · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities
Example

Worked example (availability via quorums)

Assume a system with (N_{replicas}=5) and quorum parameters (Q_w=4) (write quorum) and (Q_r=2) (read quorum).

From the book text:

  • Write availability: “a success­ful write requires that at least 4 of the 5 replicas be available.” That means if fewer than 4 replicas are reachable/available to store the write, the write cannot be confirmed by the quorum rule.
  • Read availability: “a read will succeed if only 2 of the replicas are available and agree.” That means reads can still succeed as long as at least 2 replicas are available and they agree on the data/witness value.

This illustrates how changing quorum sizes biases availability toward reads or writes during replica outages.

Slide 4: Replicated storage as one-to-many communication

What the slide says

Slide 4 contains only the number “4” and a diagram showing one left node connected by arrows to three right nodes (no labels are visible).

Slide 4
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 46%

This slide is setting up a basic replicated-storage communication pattern:

  • There is one “sending” side (the single left box) that communicates to multiple “recipient” sides (the three right boxes).
  • The arrows represent one-to-many distribution of update information so that multiple replica sites can update their own database copies.
  • This basic replicated setup is then used in later discussions of how replicas are read from and written to (often via quorum/majority-style choices), because allowing clients to contact multiple replicas can produce situations where different readers see different results unless additional mechanisms ensure coherence via some before/after atomicity.
4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Shortcuts to Meet More Modest Requirements · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book

Diagram meaning (mapping slide parts to the replicated-storage idea supported by the text):

  1. Sender node (left box)
  • In the simplest replicated storage plan discussed, there is a primary/master copy that coordinates reads and writes.
  • The master is described as being able to keep track of the ordering of read and write requests and enforce a strict consistency specification (e.g., “a read should return the result of the most recent write”).
  • That “master/primary” role is the natural interpretation of the single left box acting as the source of updates.
  1. Multiple recipient nodes (three right boxes)
  • The text describes multiple replica sites that each maintain a copy of the database.
  • The master distributes update information to these replica sites so they can bring their copies up to date.
  • The slide’s three right boxes visually correspond to multiple replica nodes.
  1. One-to-many communication (arrows from one box to several boxes)
  • The text explicitly states that “the master site can distribute just its update log to the replica sites.”
  • It also describes an enhancement where the master distributes only the parts that changed (“deltas” or “diffs”) to the replicas.
  • Both statements support interpreting the slide’s arrows as one sender distributing update information to multiple replica recipients.
  1. Why replicas need updates to stay consistent
  • After receiving the update information, the replica sites must apply it so their database copies converge.
  • One described method is that replica sites run REDO on log entries to bring their database copies up to date.
  1. Why the “how to use replicas” question matters (what later slides build on)
  • The text contrasts a simplest plan (route all client reads/writes to the primary; replicas as backups) with an enhanced plan (send reads to any replica).
  • The enhanced plan improves read availability and performance, but it creates instants during updates where “the several replicas are not identical,” so different readers can obtain different results—violating strict consistency.
  • Therefore, the system needs a mechanism that ensures “before-or-after atomicity between reads and updates,” to prevent a reader from observing an inconsistent mix of old/new replica states.
  1. Connection to quorum/majority-style reasoning
  • When reads and writes are allowed to involve subsets of replicas, quorum parameters (e.g., Nreplicas, Qw, Qr) become central.
  • The text gives an example with Nreplicas = 5, Qw = 4, Qr = 2 to show how, without sufficient atomicity, different readers could see different consistent sets even while the read/write coherence specification is not met.

Slide 5: Quorum intersection condition (R + W > N)

What the slide says

The slide shows the condition: R + W > N.

Slide 5
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 82%

The slide is pointing to a quorum configuration rule in replicated systems.

  • There are N replicas.
  • A write quorum of size W is the set of replicas that must acknowledge/hold a write before the system considers the write “confirmed.”
  • A read quorum of size R is the set of replicas a read consults that must agree on the data/witness value for the read to be successful.

The inequality R + W > N is a quorum intersection condition: if the read quorum size plus the write quorum size is greater than the total number of replicas, then a read quorum and a write quorum must overlap by at least one replica.

However, the source also emphasizes that meeting R + W > N does not automatically provide strict before-or-after (all-or-nothing) atomicity under write concurrency or crashes. A practical system needs an additional before-or-after atomicity mechanism that serializes/coordinates writes so that reads observe a coherent ordering of updates.

Slide 5 · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book · Disagreement: The slide’s rule that quorum read/write intersection is ensured by the condition

  • Meaning of the symbols (R, W, N):

    • N (number of replicas): the total replica count in the system.
    • W (write quorum size / Qw): the minimum number of replicas that must be updated/acknowledge the write for the system to consider the write confirmed.
    • R (read quorum size / Qr): the minimum number of replicas a read must query such that the returned values from those replicas agree.

  • What the inequality is trying to ensure (quorum intersection):

    • The source defines read and write quorums Qr and Qw and states they have the property Qr + Qw > Nreplicas.
    • From this, the intended effect is that any set of R replicas and any set of W replicas cannot be disjoint when R + W > N, so a read quorum will share at least one replica with the write quorum of any confirmed write.

  • How this relates to “read/write coherence” goals:

    • The source frames the quorum scheme as a way to make writes “confirmed” after reaching the write quorum and make reads “successful” when the read quorum agrees.
    • Because quorums overlap (by the R + W > N rule), the system has a basis for coherence: reads and writes are connected through shared replicas.

  • Why the slide condition alone is not enough for strict consistency under concurrency/crashes:

    • The source explicitly gives a scenario (with Nreplicas = 5, Qw = 4, Qr = 2) where the coherence requirement fails even though the quorum sizes satisfy Qr + Qw > Nreplicas.
    • In that scenario, one reader can read replicas from the “already updated” subset while another reader reads replicas from a different “not yet updated” subset, leading to different readers observing incompatible results.
    • The source concludes that a practical quorum scheme requires additional before-or-after atomicity: “serializes writes” and ensures a new write does not begin until the previous write has propagated sufficiently to ensure coherence.

  • Why this matters:

    • The quorum rule R + W > N is a structural property about quorum sizes.
    • Achieving strict “latest/most recent” behavior across concurrent operations also requires a separate mechanism to enforce correct ordering/atomic visibility (the “before-or-after atomicity” layer described in the source).
4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book · Disagreement: The slide’s rule that quorum read/write intersection is ensured by the condition
Formula
R+W>NR + W > NR+W>N
  1. R: number of replicas required for a read quorum (called Qr in the source).
  2. W: number of replicas required for a write quorum (called Qw in the source).
  3. N: total number of replicas (Nreplicas in the source).
  4. The inequality R + W > N is the quorum property the source states for separating read and write quorums.
  5. The practical takeaway described alongside this property is that overlap alone is not sufficient for coherence without an additional before-or-after atomicity mechanism.
Slide 5 · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book
Example

Example from the source showing the limits of relying only on R + W > N for coherence:

  • Parameters: Nreplicas = 5, Qw = 4, Qr = 2.
  • Quorum-sum check: Qr + Qw = 2 + 4 = 6, and 6 > 5, so the quorum intersection property (R + W > N) holds.
  • The source then describes the failure mode:
    • If an updater has updated two replicas and another reader reads those two replicas while another reader reads a different set of two replicas that the updater has not yet updated, the two readers can each believe they found a consistent set.
    • Despite each read quorum agreeing among the replicas it consulted, the overall read/write coherence specification is not met.

This illustrates that a strict coherence guarantee requires additional before-or-after atomicity/serialization beyond the quorum-size inequality.

4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Slide 5

Slide 6: Quorums (distributed replica consistency)

What the slide says

Quorums

Slide 6
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 72%

Meaning of “quorums”: In a system with multiple replicas, a quorum scheme chooses a read quorum size (Q_r) and a write quorum size (Q_w). A write is considered confirmed only after it has been written to at least (Q_w) replicas. A read is considered successful only if at least (Q_r) replicas agree on the data (or on a witness value). The scheme requires the quorum condition (Q_r + Q_w > N_{replicas}), so that any successful read intersects the replicas that must have been updated for any confirmed write. By varying (Q_r) and (Q_w), the system can bias availability toward reads or toward writes when some replicas are unavailable.

4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book

  • Why quorums exist (problem with replica reads): When reads are allowed to go to “any replica,” there can be times during an update when replicas are not identical. That can cause different readers to obtain different results, violating a strict consistency rule that a read should return the result of the most recent write.

    • Because replicas may be temporarily inconsistent during updates, restoring strict consistency requires some mechanism that ensures before-or-after atomicity between reads and updates.
    • The book notes that before-or-after atomicity is expected to “erode” the increased availability/performance gained by allowing reads to any replica.
    • (This sets the stage for using quorum rules as the mechanism for coordinating reads and writes.)

    Citations: the conflict from reading any replica and the need for before-or-after atomicity are described in W8, and the need for extra atomicity in a quorum scheme is discussed in W1/W2.

  • Core quorum definition (separate read vs write thresholds): A system can define separate read and write quorums, (Q_r) and (Q_w), rather than simply using “more than half.”

    • Write rule: “A write [is] confirmed after writing to at least a write quorum, (Q_w), of replicas.” The system continues to try to propagate the write to other replicas afterward.
    • Read rule: “A read [is] successful if at least a read quorum, (Q_r), agree on the data or witness value.”

  • Quorum intersection property (the key constraint): The quorum scheme requires:

    • (Q_r + Q_w > N_{replicas}).

    This inequality is the stated property that makes the scheme work: it is what links the minimum number of replicas used by a successful read with the minimum number required for a confirmed write.

  • Availability tuning via choosing (Q_r) and (Q_w): Because quorums are separate thresholds, varying them changes how many replicas must be available for operations to succeed.

    • One configuration can “bias availability modestly in favor of reading.”
    • Another configuration can bias availability toward writes.

    Concretely, the book gives examples on (N_{replicas}=5):

    • (Q_w=4), (Q_r=2) biases availability in favor of reading.
    • (Q_w=2), (Q_r=4) biases availability in favor of writing.

  • Important limitation: quorums alone may not guarantee strict coherence without atomicity: The book emphasizes that the quorum algorithm described (with the ability to adjust read vs write availability) “does not provide either before-or-after or all-or-nothing atomicity,” which are likely needed for strict consistency if there is write concurrency or significant crash risk.

    • It gives a specific example with (N_{replicas}=5), (Q_w=4), (Q_r=2): if one updater has successfully updated two replicas while another reader reads those two updated replicas, and a second reader reads two replicas not yet updated by the first updater, both readers can believe they found a consistent set—yet the read/write coherence specification has not been met.
    • It also gives a crash-related scenario where different updaters update different subsets, leaving “muddled” replica contents that allow different readers to observe different write subsets.

  • Therefore: additional atomicity/serialization mechanism is needed in practice: A practical quorum scheme “requires some additional before-or-after atomicity mechanism” that serializes writes and ensures no write begins until the previous write has sufficiently propagated to ensure coherence.

    • The mechanism can vary by system configuration:
      • If all reading and updating originates at a single site: a “simple sequencer” can provide atomicity.
      • If reads can come from many sources but all updates originate at a single site: the updating site can associate a version number with each update, and readers check version numbers to ensure they have read the newest consistent set.
      • If updates originate at many sites: a protocol providing a “distributed sequencer” might be needed.

  • Net meaning for the slide: The word “Quorums” on Slide 6 is pointing to this technique: using (Q_r) and (Q_w) with the constraint (Q_r + Q_w > N_{replicas}) to coordinate reads and writes over replicas, and using additional atomicity mechanisms to address cases where quorum rules alone are not enough for strict coherence.

Example

Worked example: (N_{replicas}=5), (Q_w=4), (Q_r=2) (bias toward reading)

  • Quorum sizes:

    • (N_{replicas}=5)
    • write quorum (Q_w=4)
    • read quorum (Q_r=2)

  • Quorum condition:

    • (Q_r + Q_w = 2 + 4 = 6), and (6 > 5), so the required property (Q_r + Q_w > N_{replicas}) is satisfied.

  • When a write can be confirmed:

    • A write is confirmed only after writing to at least 4 replicas.
    • Therefore, a “successful write requires that at least 4 of the 5 replicas be available.”

  • When a read can succeed:

    • A read succeeds if at least 2 replicas agree on the data (or witness).
    • Therefore, “a read will succeed if only 2 of the replicas are available and agree.”

  • Availability bias interpretation:

    • Because writing needs 4 available replicas while reading needs only 2, this configuration biases availability “modestly in favor of reading.”

  • Write availability: an update receives confirmation when it reaches at least 2 replicas (“if any two replicas are available for update”).

Slide 8: Sloppy quorum / hinted handoff (quorum-based replication with availability bias)

What the slide says

Sloppy quorum / hinted handoff

Slide 8
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 62%

“Sloppy quorum” and “hinted handoff” are replication ideas that keep the system available even when some replicas are temporarily unreachable by (1) confirming writes using only a required write quorum of replicas and (2) later repairing any differences at replicas that missed the write, using a reconciliation mechanism.

This interpretation matches the quorum framework described in the course material:

  • A quorum scheme defines separate read and write quorums, QrQ_rQr​ and QwQ_wQw​, intended to intersect enough for correctness, with the ability to tune availability by varying QrQ_rQr​ and QwQ_wQw​ in the face of replica outages.
  • In such schemes, a write is “confirmed” after reaching at least QwQ_wQw​ replicas while the system continues trying to propagate the update to the remaining replicas.
  • When updates are in progress or failures occur, replicas may temporarily diverge (because not all replicas receive updates at the same time). The material explicitly notes that the enhanced availability/quorum approach does not by itself provide strict before-or-after or all-or-nothing atomicity.
  • To address divergence, the material includes reconciliation: a procedure that compares replicas intended to be identical and repairs differences.

So the slide’s two names are best understood as: relax which replicas must be contacted immediately (to avoid write unavailability) while relying on later propagation/repair to restore coherence once the cluster situation improves.

4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book

Sloppy quorum / hinted handoff as “availability-biased quorum replication”

The slide gives only two technique names, so the meaning must be inferred from the surrounding quorum concepts presented in the evidence.

1) Quorums separate “confirmation” from “complete propagation”

The evidence explains a quorum system using read and write quorums (QrQ_rQr​ and QwQ_wQw​):

  • A write is considered successful/confirmed after it is written to at least a write quorum QwQ_wQw​ of replicas.
  • Meanwhile, the system continues to try to propagate the write to the remaining replicas.
  • A read is successful if at least a read quorum QrQ_rQr​ agree on the data/witness value. This structure directly supports an availability goal: if enough replicas for QwQ_wQw​ are reachable, the write can complete even if some other replicas are unreachable at that moment.

(These are exactly the kinds of behaviors a “sloppy quorum” idea would leverage: confirm a write without waiting for every replica, so temporary replica outage does not block writes.)

Cited support: quorum definition and “write confirmed after writing to at least a write quorum … while … propagate to the remaining replicas” (W3, W6).

2) Why relaxation can produce temporary incoherence

The evidence warns that quorum-based availability tuning can fail to guarantee strong atomicity properties by itself:

  • It states the enhanced approach “does not provide either before-or-after or all-or-nothing atomicity,” which are “likely to be required to maintain strict consistency” if there is write concurrency or significant crash risk.
  • It then provides an example with Nreplicas=5N_{replicas}=5Nreplicas​=5, Qw=4Q_w=4Qw​=4, and Qr=2Q_r=2Qr​=2:
    • If an updater has updated only two replicas so far, one reader may read the two updated replicas while another reads a different pair that the updater hasn’t reached yet.
    • Readers may each believe they saw a “consistent set,” but the overall read/write coherence specification is violated.

This shows the core tradeoff: to keep writes/reads available by contacting only quorum-sized sets, the system can expose situations where replicas do not represent one fully coherent “moment in time.”

Cited support: non-atomicity warning and the concrete contradictory-reader example (W2, W4).

3) How “hinted handoff” fits: repairing divergence (reconciliation)

The evidence includes reconciliation:

  • Reconciliation is “a procedure that compares replicas that are intended to be identical and repairs any differences.”

Under the quorum relaxation described above, replicas can temporarily diverge because a write might be confirmed after reaching only QwQ_wQw​ replicas, while propagation to others continues (and may be delayed by outages/crashes).

A “hinted handoff” style mechanism is therefore best aligned (from the evidence) with the idea that replicas which missed an update during an outage are later brought into agreement by a repair process—i.e., reconciliation once the replica can participate again.

Cited support: definition of reconciliation (W7) and the fact that the quorum scheme continues propagation rather than achieving immediate all-replica atomicity (W6, W3).

4) The overall lesson

Putting these together:

  • Quorums allow tuning availability by choosing QrQ_rQr​ and QwQ_wQw​ so operations can still succeed when some replicas are down.
  • That availability bias can come at the cost of temporarily breaking strict atomicity/consistency expectations.
  • Systems rely on additional mechanisms—explicitly including reconciliation—to restore replica agreement after transient failures and incomplete propagation.

Cited support: availability tuning by varying QrQ_rQr​/QwQ_wQw​ (W3, W4), lack of before-or-after/all-or-nothing atomicity (W4, W2), and reconciliation as repair of differences (W7).

4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book
Example

Example: quorum-based availability can produce “muddled” replica sets

Evidence provides a concrete scenario illustrating why relaxing quorum requirements can yield inconsistent observations.

Assume:

  • Nreplicas=5N_{replicas}=5Nreplicas​=5
  • Qw=4Q_w=4Qw​=4 (a write is confirmed after reaching 4 replicas)
  • Qr=2Q_r=2Qr​=2 (a read is successful if 2 agreeing replicas are found)

Now consider an updater that has begun updating and has successfully updated two replicas so far (but not yet 4).

  • One reader could read the two replicas already updated.
  • Another reader could read two replicas the updater hasn’t reached yet (if those replicas currently contain different versions).

Each reader might believe it found a “consistent set of replicas,” but the read/write coherence specification is not met.

Why this matters for “sloppy quorum / hinted handoff”: this is the kind of transient divergence that availability-biased quorum techniques must manage. The evidence’s response pathway is that reconciliation/repair mechanisms are needed to restore agreement once propagation catches up or failed replicas rejoin.

Cited support: the Nreplicas=5,Qw=4,Qr=2N_{replicas}=5, Q_w=4, Q_r=2Nreplicas​=5,Qw​=4,Qr​=2 contradictory-reader example and its “muddled set of replicas” motivation (W2, W4), plus reconciliation as repair (W7).

Slide 9: Leader-based replication/coordination (primary/leader–follower)

What the slide says

Leader-based

Slide 9
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 46%

Leader-based replication is a replication strategy where one designated node (the leader/primary) is responsible for accepting and sequencing updates, and then those updates are propagated/applied to other replicas (followers/secondaries). The key effect is that the leader/primary can enforce a strict consistency rule by tracking the ordering of requests, so clients directed to the primary can see the result of the most recent write. When propagation to followers is not instantaneous (e.g., replicas are written asynchronously), there are time instants during which replicas are not identical; during those instants, clients that read from different replicas may observe different results (violating strict consistency). If the primary fails while it is mid-update, replicas may remain inconsistent until it recovers, complicating recovery because it may be unclear which replicas are authoritative.

Slide 9 · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra · Consistency.Print.book · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities

1) What “leader-based” implies structurally (leader/primary + followers/secondaries)

  • In geographically separated replication, the text describes an approach where, when replicas are written asynchronously, one replica is identified as the primary copy, and the site that writes it is called the master; the remaining replicas are backup copies, written by slave sites. This is the primary/leader vs follower/secondary pattern implied by “leader-based.”
  • The essential structural idea: there is one designated “authoritative” copy/site for updates (the primary/leader), and other replicas (backups/followers) are updated by receiving/processing those updates.

2) Why a leader/primary helps consistency: ordering of read/write requests

  • The simplest replica plan (a master/slave system) directs all client read and write requests to the primary copy at the master site, treating slaves as backups.
  • The reason this is simple for strict consistency is that the master/primary is in a good position to keep track of the ordering of read and write requests.
  • With that ordering, it can enforce a strict consistency specification: a read should return the result of the most recent write (the “usual one for memory coherence” described in the text).

3) What changes when you use followers for reads (availability vs strictness)

  • A common enhancement is to direct reads to any replica, which improves availability (data continues to be available even when the master site is down) and can also improve performance by serving different clients concurrently.
  • The complication is that during updates there are instants when replicas are not identical. In that case, different readers may obtain different results—explicitly described as a violation of strict consistency.
  • To restore strict consistency, the text says a mechanism ensuring before-or-after atomicity between reads and updates would be needed.
  • That atomicity mechanism would likely “erode” (reduce) some of the improved availability/performance gained by reading from any replica.

4) What happens under asynchronous propagation and failures (inconsistency windows / authoritative uncertainty)

  • The asynchronous-primary/backup description makes the core timing issue explicit: when replicas are written at different times, there are instants when replicas are not identical, violating the “should be identical” constraint.
  • If a system failure occurs during one of those instants, recovery becomes more complicated because it may not be clear which replicas are authoritative.
  • Another passage states that if the primary site fails while in the middle of sending out an update, replicas may remain inconsistent until the primary site recovers.

5) Practical mitigations that relate back to leader-based coordination

  • The text lists approaches to reduce the time window during which replicas appear inconsistent to reading clients. One example given: the master holds the new version in a shadow copy; slave sites hold their shadow copies too until all replicas have successfully distributed the new version; then short messages make the shadow file the active database.
  • If the database is large, partitioning into smaller regions and assigning a different master/leader to each partition is presented as a way to distribute update work and increase availability.
  • In systems described with multiple coordinators and network problems, the lecture notes conclude with the idea of using a view server that determines which replica is the primary—addressing the risk that different components may believe different primaries, leading to replicas no longer being consistent.

How the parts relate (the “tradeoff” the slide is pointing toward)

  • Leader-based coordination supports strict consistency when clients’ reads are tied to the primary and its ordering.
  • Relaxing that by reading from other replicas (for availability/performance) or by using asynchronous propagation introduces moments where replicas diverge, which directly affects what clients can observe.
  • Failures during propagation further widen the period of inconsistency and make it harder to know which replica(s) should be treated as authoritative, unless the system has additional mechanisms to manage primary authority and reduce inconsistency windows.

Slide 10: Sync vs async (synchronous vs asynchronous replication)

What the slide says

Sync vs async

Slide 10
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 62%

This slide is contrasting two ways distributed replicas can be updated/acknowledged.

  1. Synchronous replication (coordinated propagation): the system waits until updates have been made on (at least) the required replica(s) before acknowledging success. The lecture example describes a design where the primary/leader only ACKs after it is sure the backup has all updates.

  2. Asynchronous replication (less coordinated propagation): because communication between geographically separated replicas has high latency and is unreliable, replicas are often updated asynchronously. In such designs, one site is designated as the primary copy (with others acting as backups). During the time updates are still propagating, replicas can be temporarily not identical, so a read that is allowed to go to any replica may observe different results.

The “why it matters” is consistency/atomicity: allowing reads from any replica improves availability/performance, but it creates instants during update when replicas differ, which can violate strict before-or-after atomicity / read-write coherence unless additional mechanisms (e.g., serialization or quorum/atomicity rules) are used.

Slide 10 · Computer System Engineering, Lecture 19 Availability via Replication · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities

Synchronous replication

  • The lecture replication model described uses a primary (master/leader)–backup pattern.
  • The primary chooses the order of operations and the “non-deterministic values,” so the system has a consistent ordering to apply at replicas.
  • The key coordination point is the acknowledgment rule: the coordinator is only ACKed after the primary is sure the backup has all updates.
    • This means the system’s “write success” is tied to propagation to the backup(s), so replicas are kept in sync from the perspective of when clients are told an operation completed.

Asynchronous replication

  • For geographically separated replicas, communication is problematic because it has high latency and is inherently unreliable.
  • Because of that, writing replicas synchronously is often problematic.
  • When replicas are written asynchronously, the system still organizes replicas into roles:
    • one replica is identified as the primary copy (the first one written),
    • the others are backup copies.
  • With asynchronous propagation, replicas can be temporarily inconsistent (not identical) during the period when an update has not reached all replicas.

Why “sync vs async” is really about strict consistency and atomicity

  • The book explains that a common availability/performance enhancement is to direct reads to any replica, so the system can keep serving reads even if the master site is down.
  • The complication is that during update there will be instants when replicas are not identical; then different readers may obtain different results, violating the strict consistency specification (example given: a read should return the result of the most recent write).
  • To restore strict consistency, some mechanism is needed to ensure before-or-after atomicity between reads and updates.
  • The book’s quorum discussion highlights what goes wrong when coordination/atomicity is insufficient:
    • one reader can observe only a subset of an update’s propagation while another reader observes a different subset, and both may believe they read a “consistent” set even though the global read/write coherence requirement is violated.
  • The book then states the practical takeaway: to make quorum-based replica schemes work, you need additional before-or-after atomicity that serializes writes and ensures a new write doesn’t begin until the previous one has sufficiently propagated to preserve coherence.

Bottom line

  • Synchronous: “successful write” is coordinated with replica update (ACK after backup has all updates), reducing the window where replicas differ from the client’s point of view.
  • Asynchronous: replica propagation is not fully coordinated in real time; replicas can diverge temporarily, and allowing reads from multiple replicas can expose those differences unless additional atomicity/serialization/quorum mechanisms are used.
Computer System Engineering, Lecture 19 Availability via Replication · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book
Example

Worked example from the quorum discussion (shows the coherence problem caused by incomplete/uneven propagation)

Parameters: Nreplicas = 5, Qw = 4, Qr = 2.

  1. An updater is working.
  2. The updater has successfully updated two of the replicas (not enough yet to satisfy the full quorum write requirement in the eventual steady sense).
  3. Now two different readers attempt reads:
    • Reader A reads the two replicas already updated by the updater.
    • Reader B reads two replicas that the updater hasn’t gotten to yet.
  4. Both readers can believe they have read a consistent set from their own viewpoint, because each read is based on the subset it sees.
  5. But the global read/write coherence specification is not met: the system-level “most recent write” guarantee is violated because reads are mixing views of the update’s partial propagation.

This illustrates the general hazard that motivates the slide’s sync-vs-async contrast: when propagation/coordination is not sufficient to prevent replicas from being at different update points, different clients can observe incompatible states unless the system adds a mechanism that restores before-or-after atomicity/serialization.

Slide 11: Replication lag

What the slide says

Replication lag!!

Slide 11
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 72%

Replication lag means that when a system updates replicated data, the replica copies do not become identical immediately. In geographically separated and asynchronous replication, there are “instants during update when the several replicas are not identical,” so clients that read from replicas can observe different (and therefore potentially “older”) contents depending on which replicas have already received the update and which have not. This lag can directly cause violations of strict consistency specifications unless additional mechanisms (e.g., ensuring before-or-after atomicity / using stricter read mechanisms) are used, which may reduce availability/performance.

Slide 11 · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Durable Storage and the Durability Mantra · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities · Consistency.Print.book

What the slide is trying to capture

  • The slide’s single prompt, “Replication lag!!”, is a reminder that replication is not instantaneous: during an update, replicas can temporarily differ.

Why replicas can temporarily differ (the “lag” mechanism)

  • When replicas are geographically separated, communication has high latency and is unreliable, which makes it problematic to keep replicas synchronized with synchronous writes.
  • Therefore, when replicas are made asynchronously, one replica (the first written) is treated as a primary, and the others are backup copies.
  • Under asynchronous replication, because replicas are written at different times, there are “instants during update when the several replicas are not identical.” This time difference between updating the primary and updating the backups is the essence of replication lag: replicas “catch up” gradually rather than all at once.

How this affects what clients read

  • A common enhancement is to allow reads to be directed to any replica to improve availability and performance.
  • But this enhancement has a complication: during those update instants, replicas are not identical, so different readers may obtain different results—a violation of strict consistency.
  • In other words, if a client reads from a replica that has not yet received the update, the client can observe a value that corresponds to an earlier state of the system (since other replicas have progressed further in applying the update).

What consistency requirement gets broken

  • The strict consistency example given is: a read should return the result of the most recent write (a “before-or-after” style correctness condition).
  • Replica divergence during update breaks this: different readers can see results that don’t correspond to the same point in the write timeline.

What you’d need to “fix” strict consistency (and what it costs)

  • To “restore strict consistency,” some mechanism would be needed to ensure before-or-after atomicity between reads and updates.
  • The evidence notes that adding such a mechanism “will probably erode some of the increased availability and performance” gained by reading from any replica.

A concrete example showing partial-update effects

  • With replica/quorum parameters like Nreplicas = 5, Qw = 4, and Qr = 2, the text describes a situation where:
    • One updater has updated two replicas successfully.
    • Another reader might read two replicas already updated, while another reader might read two replicas not yet updated.
    • Both readers believe they read a “consistent set,” but the system’s read/write coherence specification is violated.
  • This illustrates the same core phenomenon as replication lag: during the time window where not all replicas reflect the same update progress, different reads can observe different replica states, producing inconsistent global outcomes.

Why the slide matters for later consistency topics

  • The evidence frames replication + consistency as a trade-off: replication strategies (leader-follower, multi-leader, etc.) interact with the consistency model, ranging from strong to eventual.
  • The practical takeaway introduced by replication lag is: if replicas don’t update in lockstep, then certain consistency guarantees cannot automatically be assumed for reads from replicas unless the system uses additional coordination/selection mechanisms (and those mechanisms can reduce availability/performance).

Slide 12: Read-your-writes and Monotonic reads

What the slide says

Read-your-writes Monotonic reads

Slide 12
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 74%

The slide is introducing two client-observable consistency guarantees (weaker than full “strict consistency” across all replicas):

  1. Read-your-writes (RYW): after a client/thread has performed a write (and the system has acknowledged that write at the client-visible interface), subsequent reads by that same client should not return an older value than the one it wrote.

This is illustrated in the cache scenario where the system acknowledges completion after updating the cache’s primary replica; even though the secondary/backing copy may not yet be updated, the same thread reads from the cache and receives the updated value.

  1. Monotonic reads: successive reads by the same client should not appear to “go backward” with respect to the versions of updates they observe. The slide’s concept aligns with using version numbers and having reading sites check those version numbers to ensure they have read the newest consistent set.

Together, these are about ensuring that, at the client interface, the values/versions a client sees progress forward in time in a way that respects the client’s own past actions (RYW) and at least doesn’t regress across that client’s successive reads (monotonic reads), even while replicas may temporarily diverge globally during updates.

Slide 12 · Consistency.Print.book · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities

  • Background: why special guarantees are needed with replicas

    • When a replica system directs reads to different replicas for availability/performance, there can be instants “during update when the several replicas are not identical,” so different readers may obtain different results.
    • This violates a strict consistency rule that a read should return the result of the most recent write.
    • Full strict consistency restoration would require an additional mechanism providing “before-or-after atomicity between reads and updates,” which tends to erode availability/performance.

    Connection to the slide: Read-your-writes and monotonic reads are ways to constrain what a particular client can observe, instead of enforcing strict global read/write coherence for everyone.

    (Evidence for replica divergence and strict consistency requirement: W6, and strict consistency definition/read-from-most-recent-write: W3, W5.)

  • Read-your-writes (RYW)

    • The cache description provides the core mechanism that matches the RYW idea:
      • A non-write-through cache acknowledges a write as complete “as soon as the cache manager updates the primary replica, in the cache.”
      • The thread that performed the write can then proceed before the secondary/backing replica is updated.
      • If that same thread reads the data object “by sending a READ request to the cache,” it receives the updated value from the cache—even if the cache manager has not yet restored the invariant everywhere.
    • The key guarantee is therefore client-specific: after the client’s write is acknowledged at the cache interface, the client’s subsequent reads via that interface see the write.

    (Evidence: W5.)

  • Monotonic reads

    • To prevent a client’s successive reads from regressing to an older “consistent set,” the reading side needs a way to tell whether it has observed the newest consistent version.
    • The replica discussion describes one approach:
      • When “all updates originate at a single site,” the updating site can “associate a version number with each data update.”
      • Reading sites “can check the version numbers to ensure that they have read the newest consistent set.”
    • That requirement (checking version numbers so reads correspond to the newest consistent set) is exactly the kind of ordering constraint that produces monotonic behavior for a client’s observed sequence of reads.

    (Evidence: W8.)

  • How these guarantees relate to strict consistency

    • Strict consistency is stated as a strict interface rule: “The result of a READ… is always the value that was provided by the most recent WRITE to that object.”
    • Strict consistency hides constraint violations behind the interface, often requiring serialization/atomicity mechanisms (transactions, before-or-after/all-or-nothing atomicity).
    • RYW and monotonic reads can be seen as weaker, interface-level constraints targeted at what each client sees, implemented using mechanisms like:
      • returning updated data from the cache’s updated replica for that client (RYW), and
      • using version numbers so clients don’t observe older consistent sets later (monotonic reads).

Slide 12 · Consistency.Print.book · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replica Reading and Majorities
Example

Example for Read-your-writes (RYW) (from the non-write-through cache scenario)

  • A cache manager receives a WRITE request and updates the primary replica in the cache.
  • The system acknowledges the write as complete immediately after that cache update (without waiting for the secondary/backing update).
  • If the same thread then issues a READ request to the cache, the cache delivers the updated value.

What this demonstrates: even if replicas/backing state are not yet fully reconciled (secondary may lag), the client that performed the write does not read an older value; it “reads its own writes” through the cache interface.

(Evidence: W5.)

Consistency.Print.book
Example

Example for Monotonic reads (using version-number checking)

  • An updating site assigns a version number to each data update.
  • A reading site checks these version numbers to ensure it has read the newest consistent set.

What this demonstrates: if a client performs multiple reads over time, the version checking prevents later reads from returning data from an older “consistent set” than what was already observed earlier—so the client’s observed read sequence is monotonic with respect to update versions.

(Evidence: W8.)

What the slide says

Multi-leader ? conflicts

Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 66%

The slide is likely pointing to the replication/consistency problem that arises when there is no single leader: with multi-leader (multi-master) replication, different leaders can accept updates concurrently, so replicas can diverge temporarily (some have one update, others have another). During this divergence, readers may observe different answers depending on which replica they contact, violating a strict “read returns the most recent write” style consistency rule. Example

Worked example (quorum + concurrent update → inconsistent reads)

  • Parameters: Nreplicas = 5, Qw = 4, Qr = 2.
  • Scenario A (updater partially completed):

    1. The first updater crashes after updating two replicas.
    2. A second updater updates a different two replicas and then crashes.

    4. Reader 2 may read replicas written by updater 2.
    5. The system ends up with a “muddled set of replicas.”
  • Connection to “multi-leader conflicts” (conceptually): both scenarios show that when updates overlap with reads and replicas are not atomically updated, clients can observe different versions, which is precisely the consistency failure that “conflict” handling must resolve.

Slide 15: CAP, consistency, partition-tolerance, distributed systems

What the slide says

Slide 15 states: “CAP: a system can be consistent, available AND partition-tolerant at the same time”.

Slide 15

Distributed systems (what this slide is talking about)

  • The surrounding material describes distributed cloud systems where data is replicated across multiple machines/servers.
  • Replication is essential both for fault tolerance (surviving failures) and for performance (placing data closer to users).
  • The same material frames this as a problem of building systems from unreliable components, running across multiple machines, and staying available even through failures.

Consistency (C in CAP)

  • Replication creates a consistency challenge: copies can diverge temporarily.
  • The material states consistency as:
    • ensuring that all copies of data eventually agree, and
    • defining what clients see in the meantime while copies may not yet match.
  • The book also connects consistency to constraints on replica agreement, including the constraint that a majority (or all) replicas should be identical.

Why consistency can be hard with replication

  • Replicas can become different due to many causes; the material gives examples like:
    • replica data decaying,
    • replication algorithms aiming for eventual consistency being interrupted,
    • administrators modifying replicas in ways that break the protocol,
    • and replicas being disconnected from the network.
  • When that happens, replicas may need an after-the-fact procedure called reconciliation to discover differences and recover replica equality.

Availability (A in CAP)

  • The availability goal described in the lecture material is that distributed transaction systems should remain available even through failures.
  • The book’s replication/quorum discussion also explicitly ties availability to configuring how reads and writes succeed in the presence of replica outages:
    • Writes can be confirmed after reaching a write quorum.
    • Reads can succeed after reaching a read quorum.
    • By varying the quorum sizes, the system can bias availability toward reads or writes when replicas are down.

How quorums relate to “what clients can get”

  • The book defines:
    • A write quorum of size (Q_w): a write is confirmed after updating at least (Q_w) replicas.
    • A read quorum of size (Q_r): a read is successful if at least (Q_r) replicas agree on the data/witness.
  • It also states the key quorum property: (Q_r + Q_w > N_{replicas}), and that varying (Q_r), (Q_w) adjusts read/write availability under outages.

Partition tolerance (P in CAP)

  • The material’s replication discussion includes scenarios where replicas are disconnected from the network; during such events, replicas can drift apart and later require reconciliation.
  • The partitioning discussion in the book also describes making the system fail-soft by partitioning the data across physical devices so that failing one device compromises availability of only a portion of the data.
  • Combining replication with partitioning is described as a way to ensure continued availability if any single storage device fails, while preserving partition’s performance benefits.

CAP (what the theorem is described as doing here)

  • The provided lecture material says the “famous CAP Theorem … describes the trade-offs between Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance in distributed systems.”
  • Therefore, the slide is pointing at the idea that in replicated distributed systems, the presence of partitions/disconnections and failures forces designers to make choices that affect how well the system can satisfy consistency guarantees versus staying available.

How the consistency/availability/partition pieces connect (mechanism)

  • Replication + partitions/disconnections can cause replica divergence.
  • Quorum configuration changes:
    • whether reads/writes can complete despite outages (availability), and
    • what data different clients might observe while the system is dealing with partial replication progress (consistency).
  • The quorum example below shows a concrete failure mode of strict read/write coherence when (Q_r) and (Q_w) are not configured to match the required atomicity/coherence guarantees under concurrency/crashes.

Example

Worked example: quorum choices can lead to clients seeing different “consistent” replica sets

A specific scenario from the book shows how quorum settings can allow reads to succeed while violating a required stronger coherence property.

Given parameters

  • Number of replicas: (N_{replicas} = 5)
  • Write quorum: (Q_w = 4)
  • Read quorum: (Q_r = 2)

Case 1: an updater is in progress

  • Suppose an updater has successfully updated two of the replicas.
  • Because reads only need (Q_r = 2) agreeing replicas, one reader could read the two replicas already updated.
  • Meanwhile, another reader could read two replicas not yet updated by the in-progress updater.
  • Both readers would believe they found a consistent set (each read met the read-quorum agreement rule), but the material states the read/write coherence specification has not been met.

Case 2: an updater crashes after updating two replicas

  • With the same parameters, suppose an updater crashes after updating only two replicas.
  • A second updater might start and update a different two replicas before crashing.
  • Then a later pair of readers could observe data from the first updater’s written set versus the second updater’s written set, producing a “muddled set” of replicas.

What this illustrates relative to CAP

  • Under failure/partial progress (a kind of partition/disconnection/latency condition), quorum rules that favor availability (reads/writes can complete with a quorum) may allow clients to observe different states, harming strict consistency/coherence guarantees.

Slide 16: Vector clocks

What the slide says

Vector clocks.

Slide 16
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 68%

The slide is introducing vector clocks as a version-tracking mechanism used in distributed/replicated storage systems to support highly available writes. The idea is that replicas record enough information with each write so that, when replicas diverge (e.g., due to failures/temporary disconnection), the system can later reconcile versions during reads rather than forcing strict coordination on every write. In the referenced material, vector-clock-based approaches are described as having an advantage that version size is decoupled from update rates, meaning the amount of version metadata does not necessarily grow in proportion to how frequently updates occur.

Slide 18: Anti-entropy, Merkle trees

What the slide says

Anti-entropy Merkle trees

Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 62%

Anti-entropy (replica repair by periodic comparison): The slide’s “anti-entropy” points to a background process that prevents replica copies from diverging. The provided material describes that (1) replicas can drift apart due to random decay and updates made while already drifted, so a plan is needed to check for drift and correct it; and (2) the mechanism for identifying such differences and correcting them is called reconciliation. Reconciliation can be implemented as a module that periodically reviews the replica data to verify they are identical, and—if necessary—initiates repairs to keep them that way.

Because replicas may be geographically separated, the evidence also explains that doing “bit-by-bit comparison” is expensive (it can require transmitting a complete copy). Instead, reconciliation can use a witness: compute a hash over a replica’s contents and transmit only that witness. With a good hash and a sufficiently long witness, the probability that a damaged replica still matches the witness can be made arbitrarily small, so the witness can stand in for the replica for integrity checking and detecting loss.

Merkle trees (efficiently summarizing replica state): The slide lists “Merkle trees” as the companion topic, but the provided evidence does not explain Merkle-tree structure or how it enables partial comparisons. The evidence does, however, define the general role of hashes/witnesses in detecting differences without transmitting full data. So, from the evidence available here, Merkle trees can only be connected to the broader theme of using hash-based witnesses for efficient replica comparison; the specific mechanics of Merkle trees are not present in the supplied sources.

Slide 19: Consensus

What the slide says

Consensus

Slide 19
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 66%

The slide is introducing consensus as the core distributed-systems building block needed for making replicated state machines behave identically across multiple sites despite failures and unreliable timing/communication.

Concretely, achieving consensus means getting separated replicas to agree on (1) the values and (2) the order of inputs they should apply. This is “known as achieving consensus.” Because the replicas may lack a common clock, may crash independently, and may only communicate over a best-effort network, the difficulty is captured by a theoretical core task called the consensus problem: agreeing on a single binary value. When the assumptions allow it, consensus can be solved by specific algorithms/protocols; and if the failures/conditions are too severe, proofs show consensus can be impossible.

Once the core consensus problem can be solved, it can be bootstrapped to reach agreement on the complete set of values and order of inputs required so that a set of replicated state machines stays in sync.

4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replicated State Machines · Consistency.Print.book

1) Consensus appears because replication needs identical behavior across replicas

  • In a replicated state machine approach, the goal is that multiple replicas process the same sequence of update requests and therefore move through the same states.
  • A key requirement is: all replicas must receive the same inputs, in the same order.
  • The evidence states that agreeing on the values and order of the inputs at separated sites is known as achieving consensus.

2) Why “order” is part of consensus

  • The replicated-state-machine idea relies on the fact that if N identical state machines start from the same prior state and then receive and perform the same update requests in the same order, they enter the same new state.
  • Therefore, even if all replicas eventually get the same set of updates, differences in ordering can still cause replicas to diverge; consensus covers both agreement on what inputs/values are chosen and agreement on their order.

3) The distributed setting makes agreement hard

  • The evidence highlights difficult real-world conditions:
    • replicas do not have a common clock,
    • replicas can crash independently, and
    • sites are connected by a best-effort communication network.
  • Achieving consensus under these constraints “is a project in itself,” meaning the problem needs careful protocol design.

4) The “consensus problem” is the core theoretical abstraction

  • The evidence says theorists define the core essence of consensus as the consensus problem, whose goal is:
    • to achieve agreement on a single binary value.
  • The point of this abstraction is that it captures the essence of disagreement/coordination in the simplest form (agreement on one bit).

5) Algorithms can solve it only under specified conditions (and may be impossible under others)

  • The evidence states there are:
    • “various algorithms and protocols designed to solve this problem under specified conditions,” and
    • “proofs that with certain kinds of failures consensus is impossible to reach.”
  • So, “consensus” is not just a vague goal; it comes with a precise feasibility question depending on failures and the environment.

6) Bootstrapping: from agreeing on one bit to agreeing on a whole input sequence

  • After solving the core consensus problem (when conditions permit), the evidence says a designer can “apply bootstrapping to come to agreement on the complete set of values and order of inputs” to a set of replicated state machines.
  • This is exactly the transition from the theoretical “single binary value” task to the practical need: establishing a consistent sequence of commands/inputs that all replicas will apply in the same order.

7) How consensus fits with reconciliation in replicated state machines

  • The evidence also describes modularization for geographically separated replicas:
    • one module implements the consensus-achieving algorithm,
    • another set of modules (the state machines) performs the actual updates, and
    • a third module is responsible for reconciliation, which checks replicas are identical and initiates repairs if needed.
  • In other words: consensus is about reaching agreement on the input sequence; reconciliation is about repairing divergence of replica contents when they drift apart over time.
Consistency.Print.book · 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › 4.4: Durable Storage Revisited - Geographically Separated Replicas › Replicated State Machines
Example

Worked scenario matching the replicated state machine requirement

  • Suppose there are N identical state machine replicas and they all start from the same prior state.
  • To stay consistent, they must process update requests.
  • If the system ensures (via consensus) that every replica receives the same update requests and in the same order, then each state machine performs the updates identically, and all replicas enter the same new state.
  • If instead replicas diverge on the order (for example, one applies update #1 then #2, while another applies #2 then #1), then the requirement “receive and perform … in the same order” would be violated, so identical behavior is no longer guaranteed.

This illustrates why consensus is necessary: it is the mechanism to enforce agreement on both values and order of inputs before updates are applied.
