Slide 22: Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

What the slide says

2PC.

Slide 22
Full explanation (reconstructed from sources) · confidence 62%

Reconstruction (from surrounding provided text): The slide is introducing two-phase commit (2PC) as a transaction coordination technique used when you need all-or-nothing, before-or-after atomicity across multiple places in a system. In particular, the provided text explains that two-phase commit helps maintain constraints (invariants) even when the data involved is geographically separated.

Mechanically, the text gives a staged model: a master (acting like a coordinator) first prepares and distributes a new version while replicas hold it in a shadow copy, and only after the distributed/shadow copies are successfully in place does the system send short messages telling the replicas to make the shadow copy the active database (the “commit” step). This directly targets the issue that composite updates may cause the data to be temporarily inconsistent during intermediate steps, so the system coordinates so that the invariant is only exposed in the “committed” state.

Consistency.Print.book

What problem 2PC addresses (as described by the evidence)

  • A transaction is characterized by atomicity in the “all-or-nothing” sense and before-or-after atomicity (the effect is as if operations happened in a single serial step rather than leaving partial effects visible).
    • The provided book text states that transactions define all-or-nothing atomicity and before-or-after atomicity and are used to maintain constraints/invariants. (W4)
  • When constraints/invariants involve multiple data items stored in places that need coordinated updates, a single update action becomes composite (multiple steps).
    • During those intermediate steps, the data can temporarily violate the invariant, meaning there are times when the system’s state is not yet “safe” with respect to the constraint. (W8)
  • The evidence explicitly states that two-phase commit allows maintaining a constraint that involves geographically separated files despite communication hazards. (W8)

The core coordination idea shown in the provided text

The evidence provides an analogy to the design of 2PC using a “shadow copy” approach:

  1. Prepare / distribute phase (shadow copy stage)
    • A master site first holds the new version of the database in a shadow copy.
    • The master then asks the slave sites to do the same (hold the new version in their own shadow copies).
    • The text describes this as waiting until all replicas of the new version have been successfully distributed. (W7)
  2. Commit phase (activation stage)
    • After the distributed/shadow copies are successfully in place, the system sends short messages telling the slave sites to make the shadow file the active database. (W7)

This staged approach prevents the constraint from being violated “from the outside” by ensuring that replicas switch to the new state only after the system has reached a coordinated point.

How the slide’s “2PC” fits into the transaction/consistency story

  • The book text positions 2PC as part of the broader use of transactions for consistency realization: transactions maintain invariants and support durability and atomicity properties. (W4)
  • It then explains that maintaining a constraint across separated storage requires coordinating multiple steps and controlling when inconsistent intermediate states are exposed; 2PC is specifically mentioned as enabling constraints across geographically separated files. (W8)

What the evidence does not specify

  • The provided evidence does not explicitly list all details of 2PC such as participant voting/abort terminology or specific failure/liveness behaviors for the 2PC protocol; it only provides the shadow-copy/activation coordination model and the constraint-preservation motivation.
Consistency.Print.book
Example

Worked example (shadow-copy coordination model)

Goal: keep a constraint/invariant involving multiple geographically separated files from being violated as updates progress.

  1. A user triggers a composite update that affects more than one data item, so intermediate states during the update might temporarily break the invariant. (W8)
  2. A master site prepares the updated version in a shadow copy. (W7)
  3. The master asks each slave site to also store the updated version in its own shadow copy, i.e., to receive the new version data. (W7)
  4. The master waits until all replicas have the new version in their shadow copies. (W7)
  5. Only then, the system sends short messages to each slave to activate the shadow copy as the new active database state. (W7)

Result: replicas do not switch to the new state independently in the middle of coordination; instead, they transition to the new active state only after the coordinated preparation step is complete, supporting the goal of maintaining constraints across separated storage. (W8)
